Test Name: ID772 | EU | PLP | Flagship Use case toggle + Filter combo – regular PLP
Experiment description:
Previous PLP experiments revealed two important behavioural patterns.

First, users consistently responded to use-case and problem-based framing — Sleep, Focus, Noise. Across multiple markets, use-case categorisation influenced product selection and confirmed that meaningful need-based shopping intent already exists on the PLP. However, replacing product-based browsing entirely with use-case categorisation reduced product exploration and, in some markets, resulted in a downlift in add-to-cart rate.

Second, filter experiments showed that users actively try to refine products when given structured filters, especially with problem-based language ("Noise" outperformed "Hearing"). At the same time, forcing users into a filter-heavy journey introduced friction, fragmented navigation behaviour, and failed to improve macro conversion metrics.

Together, these experiments suggest that users want guidance and think in use cases and problems, but still want the freedom to browse and compare products directly.
This experiment introduces a hybrid PLP discovery experience that builds on both learnings:
- Product-first browsing remains the default experience
- An optional "Use cases" toggle offers a secondary navigation route for intent-driven shoppers
- A cleaner, more structured filter system is integrated into the browsing experience

The updated filter hierarchy follows a clearer decision structure: (1) Product Type, (2) Use Case, (3) Sensory refinement, (4) Color.
Critically, use case filters now surface a curated, intentional product set rather than the full catalogue. This addresses a known friction point: selecting "Noise Sensitivity" — one of our most-used filters — currently returns too many products, overwhelming users rather than guiding them. 

The curated sets are:
- Noise Sensitivity: Engage, Engage Plus, Switch (incl. Switch partnerships)
- Sleep: Eclipse, Dream
- Music & Events: Experience, Experience Plus, Switch (incl. Experience & Switch partnerships)
- Focus: Quiet, Switch (incl. Switch partnerships)
- Social Gatherings: Engage, Engage Plus, Switch (incl. Switch partnerships)
- Parenting: Engage, Engage Plus, Switch (incl. Switch partnerships)
- Travel: Quiet, Eclipse, Switch (incl. Switch partnerships)
- Playtime & Schooltime: Loop Engage Kids
- Motorcycle: Experience, Experience Plus, Switch (incl. Experience & Switch partnerships)

Note: Conversation has been removed as a standalone filter given product overlap with existing use cases.

Unlike previous experiments, users are not forced into a use-case journey or a filter-first journey. They can freely browse products directly, switch into use-case navigation, or refine through filters depending on their shopping intent.
Hypothesis:
IF we introduce an optional use-case navigation layer together with a cleaner, structured filter system on the PLP — where use-case filters surface a curated, intentional product set rather than the full catalogue — while keeping product-based browsing as the default experience,
THEN Purchase Conversion Rate (H1) and Add to Cart rate (H2) will increase or remain stable, while use-case filter engagement improves,
BECAUSE users can self-select into a need-based discovery journey when relevant, while maintaining the freedom to browse and compare directly. Reducing the number of products shown after a use-case filter is selected lowers cognitive overload and eliminates the paradox of choice effect that the current experience triggers — especially for high-traffic filters like Noise Sensitivity. Users who arrive with clear intent get a shortlist; users who are still exploring retain full access to the range. This serves both shopping modes without forcing either.

Learnings & recommendations:
Recommendation: Implement V1 as the new default. The hybrid does no harm to conversion — arguably a slight positive on revenue-per-visitor — and the restructured filter system earns its place, even though the use-case toggle itself barely gets touched.
The guardrail question is answered cleanly: adding an optional use-case layer and restructuring the filters did not damage purchase or add-to-cart. That alone clears the bar this test was designed against, and it vindicates the "wrong container, not wrong intent" reframe — offering use-case navigation as opt-in avoids the add-to-cart downlift that forcing it caused in the earlier categorisation tests. The catalogue-browsing majority is left undisturbed while intent-driven shoppers get a route if they want one.
But the toggle route is barely used, and the pattern echoes the earlier PLP toggle finding almost exactly. Around half a percent of users activated use-case mode, and of those, roughly half immediately switched back. That is not evidence of latent demand for use-case navigation as a toggle — it is the same low-activation, high-reversal signature seen before, which points to the container being wrong rather than the intent being absent. Filters, by contrast, drew more than twice the engagement of the toggle, which is consistent with the standing finding that filters and default browse logic are where use-case intent actually gets expressed. The restructured filter hierarchy is the part of this test doing the work, not the toggle.
So the honest verdict splits by component. The filter restructure and the do-no-harm-to-conversion outcome justify shipping the hybrid. The use-case toggle specifically should be treated as unproven at best and probably dead weight — worth keeping only if it costs nothing to maintain, and a candidate for removal rather than further investment. The primary KPI sits below the significance threshold, so the case for shipping rests on the guardrail pass and the revenue-per-visitor lean, not on a proven conversion win.
Management summary: The hybrid PLP held conversion flat across a full runtime — clearing the do-no-harm bar — while the use-case toggle was barely used and heavily reverted and filters drew twice the engagement, with half of filter-users stacking multiple filters, confirming for the third time that filters, not a toggle, are the container for use-case intent.

Learnings & recommendations:
Recommendation: Keep control. Iterate before re-testing.
Switch is flat on purchase (71%, below threshold) despite positive ATC, checkout and interaction signals. This is consistent with the standing Switch finding: customers can't perceive the difference between modes from static gallery imagery, so the situation-first restructure raises engagement without resolving the core "what does switching actually do for me" question. ATC and slider interaction climbing while purchase stays flat — and AOV leaning negative — is interest without conviction. Unlike Engage and Experience (multi-context products where scenarios self-explain), Switch's value is the mechanism of changing modes, which scenario imagery alone doesn't demonstrate. The named improvements target exactly this: showing the mechanism and consequence in motion rather than implying it.
Named improvements for the Switch iteration:

Test Name: ID883 | EU | PDP | Delete 640K legacy
Experiment description:
The current PDP contains a legacy section called “Join over 640K Loop fans” positioned above the comparison module. While the block was originally intended to provide social proof, recent 6V research indicates that it currently adds limited decision-making value for users. The section is not directly connected to product-specific use cases, does not help users better understand which product fits their needs, and does not function as a meaningful gateway to user-generated content or community engagement.

Additionally, the block interrupts the flow toward more conversion-oriented content such as product comparisons, specifications, and purchase-focused modules. On mobile especially, the section occupies a significant amount of vertical space, potentially pushing more relevant content further down the page and increasing unnecessary scrolling friction.

This experiment aims to validate whether removing the “Join over 640K Loop fans” block creates a cleaner and more focused PDP experience. By reducing non-essential content and keeping users concentrated on product-related information, we expect users to navigate more efficiently through the PDP and maintain stronger purchase intent throughout their journey. The test will help determine whether this legacy section still contributes value or whether it can safely be removed from the PDP template without negatively impacting engagement or conversion metrics.
Hypothesis: If we remove the “Join over 640K Loop fans” section from the PDP, then ATC (h2) and purchase (h1) will remain stable or improve, because users will experience a cleaner and more focused product page with less distraction from non-product-specific content that does not actively support purchase decision-making.
Dev briefing: Delete the 640K loopers block on all PDP's
Analysis results overview:
Purchase CVR (H1): Borderline significant uplift, 2.65% → 2.67% (+0.58%, 81% chance).
ATC rate (H2): No significant change, 5.78% → 5.80% (+0.2%, 71% chance).
AOV: No change, €57.22 → €57.55 (+0.6%, 50% chance).
RPU (per session): Moderate uplift, €1.52 → €1.54 (+1.1%, 76% chance). Inconclusive.
Checkout rate: No change, 4.16% → 4.16% (51% chance).
PLP visits: Significant uplift, 208,801 → 211,779 (+1.6% per session, 100% chance).
Learnings & recommendations:
Recommendation: Implement. Remove the "Join over 640K Loop fans" block in the Flagship PDP tests (mobile). In USA, don't leave the gap empty: keep product-specific social proof near the comparison module (star rating, review count, UGC per product). Watch US ATC closely in the Flagship PDP test.
- No harm to conversion in any region. EU and AU are borderline positive (81%). USA is flat. The block can go.
- In EU and AU, people moved on to products faster. PLP visits rose +1.6% (EU) and +1.7% (AU), both at 100% chance. The block took screen space and attention but did not help people choose. Less content before the decision means less scrolling.
- USA is the exception. ATC fell −1.5% (0% chance) and RPU fell −1.0% (4% chance). This only partly showed up in CVR. A likely reason: US shoppers rely more on "lots of people use this" as a trust signal, so the big number did work there. We have not proven this.
- AU earned more per user. RPU rose +2.3% (95%) and AOV +1.2%. A cleaner page did not push people to cheaper products.
- General brand proof ("640K fans") doesn't help people choose. Product-specific proof is the more likely job to keep, especially for USA.
Management summary: Removing the 640K fans block does no harm to conversion and helps EU and AU, but US shoppers add to cart less without it: remove it in the Flagship PDP and keep product-specific social proof for USA.
Key Results: "Run 14 experiments on flagship elements (visual, copy, interactions) across key high-traffic templates (e.g. homepage, PDP, navigation)"

Click on Yotpo Filter Rate: The variant group showed a significant downlift in filter engagement, decreasing from 0.67% to 0.49% (−26.9% downlift, 340 vs 244 clicks, 100% Bayesian chance control is better).
User Viewed Review: 52,253 in control versus 51,624 in the variant (−1.2%) — effectively identical reach into the review section. Not an exposure effect.
Learnings & recommendations:
Learnings & recommendations
Recommendation · Kill variant, iterate
What happened
Making the review module more compact cost conversion, order value and revenue at the same time. Both groups reached the review section in equal numbers and checkout rate was flat or slightly down, so the loss happened entirely inside the module. Pooled across all three markets: 93,040 control users at 9.01% CR versus 92,267 variant users at 8.78% — a 2.5% relative downlift and roughly €/$22.5K of measured revenue over 13 days on half of mobile PDP traffic.
Why it likely happened
The most likely driver is what the variant inserted above the reviews rather than what it removed below them. Control went from the star distribution straight to Search, Filters, topic chips and the first review. The variant inserted an AI summary, a “Read summary by topics” button and a seven-image media carousel before the filters, pushing the first review roughly a full mobile screen further down, while reducing first-page reviews from 5 to 3. The module became shorter overall, but the distance to the first piece of real evidence became longer — the opposite of the hypothesis.
The media carousel is the prime suspect: it is the largest added element, it sits directly in the path to the reviews, and it generated 11,327 media-scroll events in EU alone. A horizontal swipe carousel inside a vertical reading task is engaging and terminal — it feels like research and resolves nothing.
The supporting evidence is filter engagement, down 26.9% in EU, 26.5% in USA and 31.4% in AUS. Filters moved from position two, directly beneath the star bars, to position five, below the summary and the carousel, while “Read summary by topics” offered a lower-effort substitute for the same intent. Consistency at that level across three independent samples makes this the most trustworthy behavioural finding in the test. The AOV downlift in EU fits the same mechanism — reviews don’t only convert, they justify trading up to the more expensive option.
Management summary: Cleaning up the review module cost us a lot — we made it shorter by pushing the actual reviews further away. Iterate further.

Recommendation · Kill variant, iterate

Making the review module more compact cost conversion, order value and revenue at the same time. Test Name: ID933 | EU | PLP | Flagship - GST - Sticky help me choose button
Experiment description: Loop's own post-purchase (KNO) survey data shows the Help Me Choose Quiz is already a meaningful part of how customers navigate the range pre-purchase, but on the Shop All / PLP grid today it's buried — there's a static "Help me choose" card mixed in among product tiles, competing for attention with 8+ products, colour swatches, ratings, and "Tap to try" prompts. This is a classic choice-overload environment: with Dream, Quiet 2, Experience 2 (Plus), Engage 2 (Plus/Kids), and Switch 2 all visible at once, undecided visitors face a wide, low-guidance choice set with no differentiation cue beyond "Primary benefit" placeholder copy. Behavioural research on choice overload (Iyengar & Lepper) shows that as the size of a choice set grows without added guidance, decision paralysis and drop-off increase — shoppers disengage rather than choose. Persisting a "Help me choose" CTA as a sticky, always-visible element (rather than one card among many) gives undecided visitors a constant low-effort escape hatch out of the comparison grid and into a guided decision path, at the exact moment choice overload would otherwise cause them to bounce. Two destinations are tested behind the same button — the existing quiz (V1) and a product-compare view (V2) — to check whether the specific guidance tool matters or only its presence does.
Hypothesis:
IF we add a sticky, persistent "Help me choose" button/pill that stays visible on screen while scrolling the Shop All PLP grid (in addition to the static in-grid card) — testing two destinations, Variant 1 leading to the Help Me Choose Quiz and Variant 2 leading to a product-compare view,

THEN:
H1: Purchase conversion rate will increase.
H2: Add to cart rate will increase.

We'll also track click-through on the button itself as a supporting engagement metric, to see whether the guidance affordance gets used — separately from whether it converts.

BECAUSE undecided visitors facing a wide, low-differentiation choice set experience choice overload and disengage rather than commit to a product; a persistent, always-accessible guidance CTA lowers the effort cost of resolving that uncertainty at the moment it occurs, rather than requiring them to scroll back up or hunt for it among competing product tiles. Testing two destinations lets us check whether the specific tool behind the button matters, or whether the presence of guidance itself is what drives the effect.

💡 Learnings & Recommendations
What was tested: a sticky, persistent "Help me choose" button that stays visible while scrolling the PLP grid, appearing after the first product row. Today the same guidance lives as a static card buried among the product tiles; this test pulls it out into an always-available CTA. Two variants tested the destination — one leading to the Help Me Choose quiz, the other to a product-compare view — against a control with only the buried in-grid card.
Recommendation: Implement the sticky button in EU and US, where both variants delivered a strong, significant lift in purchase, order value, and revenue per visitor. Hold AUS: its negative read is most likely a small-sample, high-baseline artifact rather than evidence that guidance hurts Australian shoppers. The choice between quiz and compare can be made on maintenance cost, since the two performed near-identically everywhere.
The headline learning overturns a working assumption. Earlier in the flagship programme, guidance mechanisms looked like low-value clutter — the use-case toggle was activated by almost no one and abandoned by half of those who tried it, which suggested shoppers simply do not want navigation aids. This test shows that conclusion was too broad: it was the toggle that failed, not guidance itself. The difference is what the mechanism asks of the shopper. The toggle demanded that people re-navigate the entire page into a different mode; the sticky button offers a low-effort escape from a crowded, hard-to-differentiate grid at the precise moment hesitation sets in, without disturbing the browsing default. Same broad intent, opposite outcome — because the container and the timing are right. A persistent, in-place guidance CTA works where a mode-switch does not.
The win is not just more orders but better ones. In both winning markets, order value and revenue per visitor rose alongside conversion, not merely purchase frequency. That fits the choice-overload mechanism: undecided shoppers who are helped to a confident decision appear to commit more fully rather than defaulting to the safest, cheapest option or leaving empty-handed. The guidance is resolving genuine uncertainty, and resolved uncertainty converts at higher value.
The destination of the button barely matters. Whether it led to a quiz or a compare view, the lift was effectively the same in every market. This means the value lies in the presence and persistence of the guidance affordance, not in the specific tool behind it — which simplifies the decision and de-risks it: the ship does not hinge on getting the downstream experience exactly right.
The one real open question is whether the benefit is universal or depends on how much conversion headroom a surface has. The two markets with more room to grow both won strongly; the market with the highest existing conversion rate did not, and was clicked just as often, so lack of interest is not the explanation. This mirrors a headroom pattern seen elsewhere in the programme, where enrichment helps most where baseline conversion is weakest and fades where it is already strong. That is a useful portfolio-level hypothesis — deploy this kind of guidance to lower-converting surfaces and markets first — and a reason to treat the high-baseline market's flat-to-negative result as a ceiling effect to be retested rather than a failure to be accepted.
Management summary: A persistent "Help me choose" button lifts purchase, order value, and revenue per visitor strongly in EU and US by giving undecided shoppers a low-effort way out of choice overload at the moment of hesitation — so it ships in both, whether it leads to a quiz or a compare view makes no difference, and the single high-baseline market that didn't gain is most likely a headroom ceiling rather than a real reversal.

Test Name: ID939 | EU | PDP | Flagship - Compare module design Dream vs Quiet
Experiment description:
Both control and variant show the same comparison — Dream vs. Quiet 2 — already established as the most-compared pairing. The only thing that changes is how it's presented:
- Control: the current full compare module — two dropdown selectors (pre-set to Dream / Quiet 2), star ratings, review counts, full pricing, colorway swatches, and a "Perfect For" section per product. Visitor-facing, but dense — it reads as a research tool.
- Variant: a stripped-down "Our Most-Asked Question" card — just the two products, one line of positioning each ("Perfect for all-night sleep" vs. "Perfect for napping"), and a single "Compare them" CTA. It reads as an answer, not a task.
Because the pairing is identical, this isolates format and framing as the variable: does presenting the comparison as a lightweight, pre-answered "most-asked question" reduce the effort/weight of engaging with it, versus a full comparison table that visitors have to actively read and cross-reference?

Mechanism: the control's density is useful for Maximizers who want the full data before committing, but it's a lot of visual and cognitive load to process on a PDP — reviews, colors, pricing across two products at once. That weight can suppress engagement for visitors who'd otherwise click through, especially Satisficers who just want the doubt resolved fast. The variant compresses the same information into a low-effort teaser, using the "most-asked question" framing as social proof (other buyers had this doubt) rather than presenting it as a research task.
Hypothesis:
IF: we replace the full dual-product comparison table on the PDP with a lightweight, single-CTA "Our Most-Asked Question" card — same Dream vs. Quiet 2 pairing, different format,
THEN: click-through into the comparison (H1) and downstream purchase conversion (H2) will increase,
BECAUSE: reducing the visual and cognitive weight of the module lowers the barrier to engaging with it, so more visitors act on their curiosity/doubt instead of skimming past a dense table that reads as effort rather than resolution.

Test Name: ID940 | USA | PDP | Flagship - Compare module design Dream vs Quiet
Experiment description:
Both control and variant show the same comparison — Dream vs. Quiet 2 — already established as the most-compared pairing. The only thing that changes is how it's presented:
- Control: the current full compare module — two dropdown selectors (pre-set to Dream / Quiet 2), star ratings, review counts, full pricing, colorway swatches, and a "Perfect For" section per product. Visitor-facing, but dense — it reads as a research tool.
- Variant: a stripped-down "Our Most-Asked Question" card — just the two products, one line of positioning each ("Perfect for all-night sleep" vs. "Perfect for napping"), and a single "Compare them" CTA. It reads as an answer, not a task.
Because the pairing is identical, this isolates format and framing as the variable: does presenting the comparison as a lightweight, pre-answered "most-asked question" reduce the effort/weight of engaging with it, versus a full comparison table that visitors have to actively read and cross-reference?

Mechanism: the control's density is useful for Maximizers who want the full data before committing, but it's a lot of visual and cognitive load to process on a PDP — reviews, colors, pricing across two products at once. That weight can suppress engagement for visitors who'd otherwise click through, especially Satisficers who just want the doubt resolved fast. The variant compresses the same information into a low-effort teaser, using the "most-asked question" framing as social proof (other buyers had this doubt) rather than presenting it as a research task.
Hypothesis:
IF: we replace the full dual-product comparison table on the PDP with a lightweight, single-CTA "Our Most-Asked Question" card — same Dream vs. Quiet 2 pairing, different format,
THEN: click-through into the comparison (H1) and downstream purchase conversion (H2) will increase,
BECAUSE: reducing the visual and cognitive weight of the module lowers the barrier to engaging with it, so more visitors act on their curiosity/doubt instead of skimming past a dense table that reads as effort rather than resolution.

Test Name: ID943 | All regions | Sitewide, Footer | Flagship | Move country + language switcher: header to footer (mobile)
Experiment description:
The mobile header currently carries a country flag that opens a Country + Language modal. It occupies premium header real estate for a low-frequency action — most users never change locale, as it's geo-detected on entry. We want that space for a higher-value element (AI Search).

A near-identical control already lives in the footer, which is the conventional location users look for locale switching. 

The only functional gap: the footer selector handles country + currency but not language. 

By routing the footer selector to the same modal the header flag triggers today, we consolidate locale control into one place, lose zero functionality, and free the header — without building anything new.

This is a do-no-harm (non-inferiority) test: we're proving removal doesn't hurt, not chasing a lift.
Hypothesis:
IF we remove the country flag from the mobile header and route the existing footer locale selector to the same Country + Language modal (footer label updated to show country · currency · language),
THEN purchase conversion rate (H1) will hold flat or improve, with no drop in checkout completion for international / non-primary-market traffic (guardrail),
BECAUSE locale switching is a rare, geo-detected action that belongs in the footer by convention; users who need it will still find it there, and no user loses the ability to change country, currency, or language.

Test Name: ID945 | EU | PDP | Flagship - Content - Full Content vs. No Content vs. Progressive Reveal
Experiment description:
Testing: Whether removing or shortening the product description block changes purchase behaviour, across all earplug PDPs (Dream, Quiet 2, Experience 2 + Plus, Engage 2 + Plus/Kids, Switch 2, McLaren Switch).

Control: Current full expandable content (benefit checklist + "show more").
Var 1 — No content: Hides the content block entirely. Nothing else changes or gets replaced — the page is just shorter, everything below moves up.
Var 2 — Progressive reveal: Shows only the first paragraph, no expand/collapse. Includes a scroll-triggered animation — text opacity shifts grey → black as the user reads down it. No other elements added.

What this isolates: Content volume and presentation are the only variable. Layout, ATC placement, and Compare link position stay constant everywhere else on the page.
Hypothesis:
IF we hide the product description content entirely (Var 1) or shorten it to a single animated paragraph (Var 2),

THEN purchase CVR (H1) & Add to cart (H2) will hold flat or improve in Var 2 but decline in Var 1, consistently across product lines,

BECAUSE the content block currently carries reassurance signals (comfort claims, ear-tip specifics, fit guidance) that reduce pre-purchase uncertainty — a real barrier here given fit is the top negative-review driver for Dream (46%) and ANC-expectation gap is a known issue for Quiet 2 (138 reviews). Removing it outright (Var 1) strips that reassurance with nothing replacing it, which should increase hesitation or perceived risk at the point of decision (BOOM: Certainty friction). Var 2 keeps enough content to preserve the reassurance signal while reducing the reading/scanning effort (Ability friction) needed to get there; the grey-to-black animation is a light engagement mechanic that should pull more users through the shortened paragraph than they'd read of the full expandable block, without adding any new page elements.

Analysis results overview:
Purchase CR: Variation 1 (No Content) showed no uplift in Purchase CR, holding flat at 3.28% in both control and variant (0% change, 51% Bayesian chance to win) — a dead heat. Variation 2 (Progressive Reveal) showed a moderate uplift in Purchase CR, increasing from 3.28% in control to 3.32% in variant (+1.3% uplift, 80% Bayesian chance) — right at the decision threshold, worth watching but not yet callable.

ATC Rate: Variation 1 showed a moderate uplift in Add To Cart Rate, from 7.09% to 7.17% (+1.1% uplift, 87% Bayesian chance). Variation 2 showed a similar moderate uplift, from 7.09% to 7.16% (+0.99% uplift, 83% Bayesian chance).

AOV: Both variants showed no uplift in AOV (€54.66 → €54.48 and €54.78, both 50% Bayesian) — flat, as expected since content changes rarely move basket size directly.

Supporting metrics: Checkout Rate is inconclusive for both variants (66% and 32% Bayesian). Visits to PLP dropped in both variants (-2.2% at 82%, -3.9% at 11%) — directionally, users are backtracking to PLP less, consistent with content resolving purchase decisions on-page rather than sending people back to compare.

Combined view from 3 regions
What's broken
- 🔴 Engage 2 — worst line. −12.3% USA, down in all three markets. EU+USA −5.1%.
- 🔴 Engage Kids 2 — −11.7% USA, −12.3% AUS. Fine in EU.
- 🔴 Experience 2 — down in both decision markets, in both variants. EU+USA −3.5%.
- 🔴 Quiet 2 — soft everywhere, worst in USA at −6.3%.
- ✅ Dream — up in all three markets.
- ⚠️ Switch 2 — big win in EU and USA, big drop in AUS. See below.
One cause, seen in the copy: the kept paragraph is now the whole description, but on these four products it doesn't say who it's for, how much noise it blocks, or how it differs from the next product along. Dream's paragraph does all three — and Dream is the only product up everywhere.

Switch 2 — market split flag
- EU: +97 units (+€5.0k), +7.8%
- USA: +37 units (+$2.0k), +3.6%
- AUS: −66 units (−$5.3k), −21.1%
- EU+USA combined: +5.8% units, 97% chance to win — clear win where the volume is
- AUS is down in both variants (V2 −21.1%, V1 −17.1%), so not easily dismissed as noise — but it is only ~300 units per arm in a market already below our 2,500 conversion rule
- Action: do not block on this. Add Switch 2 AUS units as a named check in the flagship test read-out. If the drop repeats at this size, review the AU Switch 2 page.
Learnings & recommendations:
Recommendation: 
- Implement Variation 2 (Progressive Reveal) in the Flagship PDP tests - using the updated improved copy (as planned)
    - We can be confident in the latest design because:
        - the copy is updated and improved 
        - there are many more supporting items below, that help do the job that the control content area did
        - If any Big PDP tests underpeform - check if any content is missing in the Control content section vs the new full page design
- Kill Variation 1 (No Content).

What we learned across all 3 regions
- Shortening PDP content doesn't harm conversion, but it isn't neutral per product. 
    - V2 was positive in EU (+1.2%) and AUS (+2.1%), and flat in USA (−1.3%, not significant). 
        - Underneath that, Dream and Switch 2 gained
        - while Engage 2, Experience 2 and Quiet 2 lost. 
    - V1 stripped the content out entirely and gained nothing in any market.
- One paragraph is enough only if it answers three things: who it's for, how much noise it blocks, and why not the product next to it. Dream's paragraph does all three and gained in every market. 
    - Engage 2, Experience 2 and Quiet 2 don't, and all three lost (this is handled in big PDP flagship test)
- A rising AOV can be a bad sign. In USA it rose because cheaper products stopped selling, not because baskets grew.
- Traffic splits must be corrected before reading product sales. Raw numbers made all six arms look like losses.
    - Relevant to any A/B/C test
Management summary: Progressive reveal (V2) is safe to ship. Overall positive in EU and AUS, not significantly down in USA. Losses were concentrated in Engage 2, Experience 2 and Quiet 2, due to the copy - the flagship PDP designs already fix this with new copy and a "Is Loop X for me?" block, so no further action needed before the full page test.

Test Name: ID948 | EU | Homepage | Flagship - Usecase Entry Navigation Below Homepage Hero
Experiment description:
Control: Current homepage — hero banner (e.g. Tomorrowland x Experience) flows directly into next section (bestseller carroussel)
Variant 1: A "What brings you here?" situational entry point placed directly below the hero — six use-case tiles (Focus, Sleep, Events, Kids, Everyday, Calm), each with a lifestyle photo and arrow affordance, plus a "Help me choose" CTA (quiz entry) beneath. Tiles link to a filtered PLP.
Variant 2: Same "What brings you here?" module as Variant 1 — same tiles, same photos, same "Help me choose" CTA — but tiles link directly to a single PDP instead of a filtered PLP.
Hypothesis:
IF we replace/precede the standard product-first navigation with a situation-first entry list directly below the hero — testing two destinations behind the tiles, Variant 1 linking to a filtered PLP and Variant 2 linking directly to a PDP,

THEN we will see an increase in PDP/PLP click-through and downstream purchase CVR,

BECAUSE Loop customers shop by situation, not by product name — the "product confusion" problem stems from a confidence gap, not a comparison gap. Letting a first-time visitor self-select by why they're here (sleep, focus, kids, etc.) removes the cognitive load of having to first map their need onto Loop's product naming/nomenclature, before they've even understood the category. Testing both destinations checks whether the landing experience after the click matters as much as the entry point itself — a filtered PLP still lets the visitor compare, while a direct-to-PDP route removes that step entirely.

H1 (Primary): Purchase CVR — situational entry reduces early-funnel drop-off caused by not knowing "which Loop is for me," so more sessions convert.
H2 (Confirmatory/Engagement): Click-through rate on use-case tiles + quiz start rate on "Help me choose" — validates that the mechanism (situational self-selection) is actually being used, not just present.

The block works as an entry point. Roughly a third of all mobile visitors clicked one of the five usecases — 32-34% in Variation 1 and 36-41% in Variation 2 — and that number is almost identical in EU, USA and AUS. People want to enter the site through their own problem rather than through a product. That part of the hypothesis is confirmed and the block should stay.
The problem is not the click. It is what happens after it.
In Variation 1 the block pushes a lot of extra traffic to the PLP: PLP visits rose 62% in EU, 91% in USA and 65% in AUS. But that traffic converts far worse than normal PLP traffic — Amplitude confirms the PLP conversion rate in Variation 1 is well below control. So we are not losing people on the homepage, we are losing them on the landing page. They arrive on a page that does not confirm what they just clicked: no matching title, no filter applied, and a range that is missing the partnership and Plus products. Someone clicks "Sleep" and gets a generic overview, so they have to start choosing all over again.
In Variation 2 the same problem shows up in a different shape. The block is identical in both variants up to the moment of the click, yet Variation 2 records more clicks per category in 14 of the 15 category-region combinations, up to +54%. Those are click-backs: visitors land on one pre-selected product page, see it is not the product they need, go back to the homepage and click another usecase. The categories with the most click-backs are exactly the ones where the right product is least obvious — Focus (+27% to +54%) and Sensitivity (+10% to +30%) — while Sleep (+3% to +8%) and Kids (0% to +11%) barely show it, because those have one clear answer. Sending people straight to a single PDP removes the comparison they still need to make.
AOV is down, most likely because bestsellers moved down the page. EU -2.5% and -2.2%, USA -2.2% and -1.8%. The usecase block helps people navigate but it does not sell anything; the bestsellers block does. Pushing it further down the homepage costs order value. AUS is the exception, where AOV went up instead — which fits, because Loop Dream dominates that market anyway (Sleep is the top usecase there at 12-13%), so less bestsellers visibility costs less.
Keep the current order. Pooled over all six variant groups (104,971 users, 36,590 clicks) the usage matches the order we tested: Sleep 10.1%, Sensitivity 9.5%, Events 8.7%, Focus 4.3%, Kids 2.2%. Worth noting that this ranking is partly a result of the order we showed, so it cannot be read as pure preference — which is another reason not to reshuffle on this data alone. USA is the one real exception: there Events is the most clicked usecase (9.87%) and Sleep only third (7.24%), and Events won that from third position, so the demand is genuine. Move Events to first for USA only, after BFCM, so we leave the homepage alone during peak.
One thing that makes the case stronger: USA already won on conversion (+8.4%, 99% chance) with the broken PLP landing in place. Whatever the fix is worth, it is worth more than what we measured.
Recommendation: Iterate
Take this into the final homepage test with three changes:
1. Add a variant where the usecase block sits below the bestsellers block instead of above it, so we can separate the navigation gain from the AOV loss and see whether the loss is purely a position effect.
2. Clean up the PLP landing in every variant: a title that matches the usecase that was clicked, the matching filter already selected on arrival, and the partnership and Plus products added to the range so the selection is complete.
3. Keep the current usecase order. Plan the USA switch to Events-first as a separate change after BFCM.
Management summary: One in three mobile visitors clicks the usecase block, so the need-based entry point works — we are losing them on the landing page after the click, not on the homepage.

Variant 1: A "What brings you here?" situational entry point placed directly below the hero — six use-case tiles (Focus, Sleep, Events, Kids, Everyday, Calm), each with a lifestyle photo and arrow affordance, plus a "Help me choose" CTA (quiz entry) beneath. Tiles link to a filtered PLP.
Variant 2: Same "What brings you here?" module as Variant 1 — same tiles, same photos, same "Help me choose" CTA — but tiles link directly to a single PDP instead of a filtered PLP.
Hypothesis:
IF we replace/precede the standard product-first navigation with a situation-first entry list directly below the hero — testing two destinations behind the tiles, Variant 1 linking to a filtered PLP and Variant 2 linking directly to a PDP,

THEN we will see an increase in PDP/PLP click-through and downstream purchase CVR,

BECAUSE Loop customers shop by situation, not by product name — the "product confusion" problem stems from a confidence gap, not a comparison gap. Letting a first-time visitor self-select by why they're here (sleep, focus, kids, etc.) removes the cognitive load of having to first map their need onto Loop's product naming/nomenclature, before they've even understood the category. Testing both destinations checks whether the landing experience after the click matters as much as the entry point itself — a filtered PLP still lets the visitor compare, while a direct-to-PDP route removes that step entirely.

H1 (Primary): Purchase CVR — situational entry reduces early-funnel drop-off caused by not knowing "which Loop is for me," so more sessions convert.
H2 (Confirmatory/Engagement): Click-through rate on use-case tiles + quiz start rate on "Help me choose" — validates that the mechanism (situational self-selection) is actually being used, not just present.

Analysis results overview:
Purchase Conversion Rate (H1): The variant group (Variation 1 – to PLP) showed a downlift in purchase conversion rate, decreasing from 12.96% in the control group to 12.48% in the variant group (-3.7% downlift, 77% Bayesian chance of a downlift, CI -12.74% to +6.24%) — inconclusive, just below threshold. Variation 2 (to PDP) was flat at 12.91% (-0.4% downlift, 53% Bayesian chance of a downlift, CI -9.69% to +9.88%) — inconclusive.
Add to Cart Rate (H2): Variation 1 decreased from 21.20% in the control group to 20.57% (-3.0% downlift, 79% Bayesian chance of a downlift) — inconclusive, just below threshold. Variation 2 showed a significant uplift to 22.12% (+4.3% uplift, 88% Bayesian chance).
AOV: Both variant groups showed a significant uplift in AOV. Variation 1 increased from $88.92 in the control group to $92.05 (+3.5% uplift, 96% Bayesian chance); Variation 2 increased to $91.38 (+2.8% uplift, 91% Bayesian chance). This is the opposite direction from EU and USA.
Revenue per Visitor (PSV): Variation 1 was flat, moving from $11.53 in the control group to $11.49 (-0.3% downlift, 45% Bayesian chance of a downlift). Variation 2 increased to $11.80 (+2.3% uplift, 70% Bayesian chance). Both inconclusive.
Checkout Rate: Variation 1 decreased from 19.68% in the control group to 19.50% (-0.9% downlift, 60% Bayesian chance of a downlift) — inconclusive. Variation 2 showed a significant uplift to 20.49% (+4.1% uplift, 85% Bayesian chance).
Product Detail Views (PDV): Variation 1 decreased from 58.06% in the control group to 55.23% (-4.9% downlift, not reported). Variation 2 showed a significant uplift to 66.16% (+14.0% uplift, 100% Bayesian chance).
Visits to PLP Rate: Variation 1 showed a significant uplift, increasing from 33.74% in the control group to 55.65% (+64.9% uplift, 100% Bayesian chance). Variation 2 showed a significant downlift to 32.90% (-2.5% downlift, 82% Bayesian chance of a downlift).
Visits to PDP Page Rate: Variation 1 decreased from 82.56% in the control group to 79.39% (-3.8% downlift, not reported). Variation 2 showed a significant uplift to 92.12% (+11.6% uplift, 100% Bayesian chance).
Usecase block engagement (variant-only): 34.3% of Variation 1 users clicked a usecase entry (Sleep 12.08%, Sensitivity 8.25%, Events 7.98%, Focus 3.32%, Kids 2.68%). Variation 2: 40.6% (Sleep 13.05%, Sensitivity 10.69%, Events 9.02%, Focus 5.11%, Kids 2.68%) — the highest engagement of the three regions.
Learnings & recommendations:
The block works as an entry point. Roughly a third of all mobile visitors clicked one of the five usecases — 32-34% in Variation 1 and 36-41% in Variation 2 — and that number is almost identical in EU, USA and AUS. People want to enter the site through their own problem rather than through a product. That part of the hypothesis is confirmed and the block should stay.
The problem is not the click. It is what happens after it.
In Variation 1 the block pushes a lot of extra traffic to the PLP: PLP visits rose 62% in EU, 91% in USA and 65% in AUS. But that traffic converts far worse than normal PLP traffic — Amplitude confirms the PLP conversion rate in Variation 1 is well below control. So we are not losing people on the homepage, we are losing them on the landing page. They arrive on a page that does not confirm what they just clicked: no matching title, no filter applied, and a range that is missing the partnership and Plus products. Someone clicks "Sleep" and gets a generic overview, so they have to start choosing all over again.
In Variation 2 the same problem shows up in a different shape. The block is identical in both variants up to the moment of the click, yet Variation 2 records more clicks per category in 14 of the 15 category-region combinations, up to +54%. Those are click-backs: visitors land on one pre-selected product page, see it is not the product they need, go back to the homepage and click another usecase. The categories with the most click-backs are exactly the ones where the right product is least obvious — Focus (+27% to +54%) and Sensitivity (+10% to +30%) — while Sleep (+3% to +8%) and Kids (0% to +11%) barely show it, because those have one clear answer. Sending people straight to a single PDP removes the comparison they still need to make.
AOV is down, most likely because bestsellers moved down the page. EU -2.5% and -2.2%, USA -2.2% and -1.8%. The usecase block helps people navigate but it does not sell anything; the bestsellers block does. Pushing it further down the homepage costs order value. AUS is the exception, where AOV went up instead — which fits, because Loop Dream dominates that market anyway (Sleep is the top usecase there at 12-13%), so less bestsellers visibility costs less.
Keep the current order. Pooled over all six variant groups (104,971 users, 36,590 clicks) the usage matches the order we tested: Sleep 10.1%, Sensitivity 9.5%, Events 8.7%, Focus 4.3%, Kids 2.2%. Worth noting that this ranking is partly a result of the order we showed, so it cannot be read as pure preference — which is another reason not to reshuffle on this data alone. USA is the one real exception: there Events is the most clicked usecase (9.87%) and Sleep only third (7.24%), and Events won that from third position, so the demand is genuine. Move Events to first for USA only, after BFCM, so we leave the homepage alone during peak.
One thing that makes the case stronger: USA already won on conversion (+8.4%, 99% chance) with the broken PLP landing in place. Whatever the fix is worth, it is worth more than what we measured.
Recommendation: Iterate
Take this into the final homepage test with three changes:
1. Add a variant where the usecase block sits below the bestsellers block instead of above it, so we can separate the navigation gain from the AOV loss and see whether the loss is purely a position effect.
2. Clean up the PLP landing in every variant: a title that matches the usecase that was clicked, the matching filter already selected on arrival, and the partnership and Plus products added to the range so the selection is complete.
3. Keep the current usecase order. Plan the USA switch to Events-first as a separate change after BFCM.
Management summary: One in three mobile visitors clicks the usecase block, so the need-based entry point works — we are losing them on the landing page after the click, not on the homepage.
Key Results: "Run 14 experiments on flagship elements (visual, copy, interactions) across key high-traffic templates (e.g. homepage, PDP, navigation)"

Test Name: ID951 | EU | Homepage | Flagship - Bestseller Block Format — Carousel vs. Stacked
Experiment description:
Control: Current homepage bestseller block ("Most loved earplugs") — horizontal carousel (Slide), one card visible at a time, swipe/arrow to advance, dot pagination indicating additional cards exist off-screen. The full card tile is clickable.
Variant 1 (Carousel): Same carousel interaction pattern as control, but the clickable area is restricted to the product image and product name only — not the full tile.
Variant 2 (Stacked): A stacked layout (Stack), where the second product card is partially visible below the first, removing the need to swipe to discover it exists. Same restricted click area as Variant 1 (image and name only, not full tile).
This test isolates two things at once: interaction pattern (carousel vs. stacked) and click target size (full tile vs. image/name only), since both variants share the smaller click target against a control with a fully clickable tile.
Hypothesis:
IF we present the Loop Essentials bestseller block as a stacked card format instead of a horizontal carousel,

THEN: 
H1 (Primary): Purchase CVR will increase.
H2 (Secondary): Add to cart rate will increase.

We'll also track CTR on the bestseller block (per-card, not block-level) and % of sessions that engage with the second/third product, as supporting engagement metrics — these confirm whether stacking actually surfaces content the carousel hides, separate from whether it converts.

BECAUSE carousels rely on an implicit promise that users will swipe to discover more content — but this promise is frequently broken (banner blindness / carousel fatigue means most users never interact past the first slide). A stacked format makes the existence of additional products physically visible at rest (peeking edge, offset card) without requiring an interaction to reveal it, lowering the ability threshold to discover the second product.
Analysis results overview:
Conversion Rate:
Variant 1 (Carousel) showed a significant uplift in conversion rate, with an increase from 9.18% in the control group to 9.74% in the variant group (+6.1% uplift, 99% Bayesian chance). Variant 2 (Stacked) rose to 9.28% (+1.1% uplift, 67% Bayesian chance), which is below our 80% threshold and therefore not conclusive.
Transactions:
Transactions increased from 2,839 in the control group to 2,963 in Variant 1, while Variant 2 landed at 2,834. Traffic was balanced across arms at 30,921, 30,413 and 30,525 users respectively.
Average Order Value:
AOV was effectively flat in both variants. It moved from €55.02 in the control group to €55.55 in Variant 1 (+1.0% uplift, 50% Bayesian chance) and €55.82 in Variant 2 (+1.5% uplift, 50% Bayesian chance). The conversion gain is therefore not coming from larger baskets.
Revenue per User:
Variant 1 achieved a significant uplift in revenue per user, rising from €5.05 in the control group to €5.41 (+7.1% uplift, 98% Bayesian chance). Variant 2 reached €5.18 (+2.6% uplift, 65% Bayesian chance), not conclusive.
Revenue:
Total revenue increased from €156,202 in the control group to €164,584 in Variant 1 and €158,190 in Variant 2.
Product Detail View Rate:
Both variants drove significantly more users onto product pages. PDV rate rose from 54.37% in the control group to 57.48% in Variant 1 (+5.7% uplift, 100% Bayesian chance) and 56.13% in Variant 2 (+3.2% uplift, 100% Bayesian chance).
PLP Visit Rate:
Category page traffic increased significantly in both variants. PLP visits per user rose 12.2% in Variant 1 and 6.1% in Variant 2, both at 100% Bayesian chance.
Checkout Rate:
Checkout rate increased significantly in both variants, from 13.76% in the control group to 14.73% in Variant 1 (+7.0% uplift, 100% Bayesian chance) and 14.52% in Variant 2 (+5.5% uplift, 100% Bayesian chance).
Add to Cart Rate:
Add to cart rate did not move meaningfully. It went from 16.75% in the control group to 16.91% in Variant 1 (+1.0% uplift, 71% Bayesian chance) and 16.70% in Variant 2 (-0.3% uplift, 45% Bayesian chance).
Bestseller Block CTR:
Click-through on the bestseller block itself dropped substantially in both variants, from 15.62% in the control group to 9.78% in Variant 1 (-37.4%) and 13.02% in Variant 2 (-16.6%). In absolute clicks that is 4,830 in control against 2,973 and 3,973. This is the expected mechanical effect of the smaller click target and is not a Bayesian-tested goal in this report.
Learnings & recommendations:
Implement Variant 1 (Carousel) in EU, USA and AUS, exactly as tested — only the product image and product name clickable, not the full tile. We keep it that way for the big test as well. Making the tile fully clickable would ship a configuration we never measured, and the evidence suggests the smaller click target is part of why this variant wins, so we are not taking that risk now. We retest fully clickable after BFCM as its own experiment.
Learnings:
Both new formats beat the current block, so this was not a choice between a winner and a loser. Pooled across the three markets the carousel delivered +4.2% purchase CR at 98.5% Bayesian chance; the stacked format reached +1.5% at 78% and sits below our threshold. EU is a standalone winner (+6.1%, 99%), while USA and AUS lacked traffic rather than lacked the effect — every regional interval contains the pooled result. Build the business case on roughly +4%, not the +6.1% EU headline.
The clearest finding is behavioural. Both formats cut clicks into the bestseller block by 17% to 40%, yet increased product detail views by around 3 percentage points and PLP visits per user by 6% to 15%, at 100% Bayesian chance in five of six cells. The block became a worse click magnet and a better navigation entry point. USA is the internal control on that reading: the stacked variant there is the only cell where block CTR held flat, and also the only cell where PDV and PLP visits did not rise.
Management summary: The carousel bestseller block lifted purchase CR by +4.2% across EU, USA and AUS (98.5% chance to win) by pulling clicks out of the block and pushing users onto product and category pages instead — we ship it exactly as tested with the smaller click target and only retest full-tile clickability after BFCM.
Key Results: "Run 14 experiments on flagship elements (visual, copy, interactions) across key high-traffic templates (e.g. homepage, PDP, navigation)"

Test Name: ID954 | EU | Homepage | Homepage Hero Format — Carousel vs. Stacked vs. Hybrid
Experiment description:
The current homepage hero is a single carousel slot — one campaign banner visible at a time (e.g. Halo, then Tomorrowland x Experience, then McLaren Racing), with the visitor needing to swipe or wait for auto-rotation to see the others. This test isolates hero format as the sole variable — same banners, same copy, same imagery, same order — testing two alternative structures against the current carousel:

Test Name: ID957 | EU | Cart | Flagship - Native Express Payment Button + Order Summary in Cart Sticky Footer
Experiment description:
Control (current live cart): the cart footer is sticky — it stays pinned to the bottom of the screen. It shows the shipping line, the subtotal, and one "Continue to Checkout" button. No express payment options.

V1: the same sticky footer as in Control, plus a row of express payment options under "Continue to Checkout", labelled "or buy directly". Up to 3 options show, depending on the device and browser (Shop Pay, PayPal, Google Pay, Apple Pay). Nothing else on the cart changes.

V2: the same express payment row as V1, but the footer is no longer sticky. It sits at the end of the cart content, so people scroll to reach it. Because of this, the "You may also like" cross-sell block is always fully visible. In Control and V1 the sticky footer can cover part of it, depending on how many items are in the cart.
Hypothesis:
IF we add express payment options under the "Continue to Checkout" button in the cart footer ("or buy directly": Shop Pay, PayPal, Google Pay or Apple Pay, shown based on the device), and we test that footer both sticky (V1) and non-sticky (V2),

THEN purchase conversion rate will go up (H1) and average order value will stay flat or go up (H2),

BECAUSE express payment takes away the work of filling in a form at the exact moment people are most ready to buy. Decisive shoppers can skip the steps completely. Hesitant shoppers get an easier, safer-feeling way to finish: a payment sheet with Face ID, Touch ID and a saved card beats typing card details into a web form, and the wallet logos are familiar. This test is mobile only, where typing is hardest of all. We do not expect express payment to lift order value on its own, so AOV is here as a do-no-harm check.

Test Name: ID960 | EU | Cart | Flagship - USP Reassurance Row Below Line Items in Cart
Experiment description: What the change will be: Control (current live Cart page): product line item shows only image, name, variant, quantity selector, and price — no reassurance copy below the item. Variant: below product item, add a small reassurance row with two icon+text USPs — "100-day trial" and "2-year warranty" — matching the placement in the screenshot. No other cart elements change (free shipping bar, quantity controls, pricing all stay as-is).
Hypothesis:
IF we add "100-day trial" and "2-year warranty" USP reassurance below each product line item in the cart,

THEN we will see an increase in Cart → Purchase conversion rate,

BECAUSE surfacing risk-reversal signals at the point where price is most visible reduces purchase anxiety and loss aversion (the fear of committing to a wrong purchase) right before the moment shoppers decide whether to proceed to checkout, particularly for higher-anxiety or first-time buyers who haven't seen this reassurance since the PDP.

Note: please use "100-day trial" (not "100-night trial" as shown in the screenshot)
Analysis results overview:
Transactions (H1): The variant showed no significant uplift in transactions, increasing from 6,926 in control to 6,982 in variant (+0.70% uplift, 67% Bayesian chance) — below the 80% threshold, inconclusive.
Add To Cart Rate (H2): Flat. Both control and variant sit at 16.92%, with only a marginal shift in Bayesian split (48% control vs. 52% variant) — no real signal either direction.
AOV: No difference. €55.46 in control vs. €55.79 in variant, sitting at a 50/50 split — pure noise.
PSV: Moderate, inconclusive uplift from €5.28 to €5.34 (64% Bayesian chance) — below threshold.
Checkout Rate: This is the flag. Control's checkout rate (14.18%) beat variant's (14.03%) with 80% Bayesian chance — right at the decision threshold, meaning there's a real (if borderline) signal that the reassurance row hurts checkout completion in EU.
Visits to PLP: Excluded — not hypothesis-relevant for this test.
Learnings & recommendations:
Most EU metrics are genuinely neutral — transactions (+0.70%, 67%), ATC (flat), AOV (flat) all sit in true no-signal territory, which is exactly what "do no harm" is designed to wave through. But checkout rate is not neutral — it's a directional negative at 80% Bayesian chance that control beats variant (14.18% vs. 14.03%). That's not an absence of a signal, it's a signal of harm, landing right at the same threshold we'd use to call a positive result significant. Treating it as noise because the primary metric (transactions) is flat would be inconsistent — if 80% is high enough to call USA's checkout rate a win, it's high enough to take EU's checkout rate warning seriously.

Recommendation: Implement in EU too, but flag checkout rate as a watch-item post-launch, rather than blocking on it — since it's borderline and low-cost to monitor at flagship scale rather than gatekeeping the rollout on one secondary metric. If checkout rate confidence climbs above 80% on more traffic post-launch, that's the trigger to revisit, not the current data.
Management summary: Adding the "100-day trial" and "2-year warranty" reassurance row to the cart is genuinely neutral on transactions in EU — but checkout rate came in lower for the variant at 80% chance, worth watching post-launch rather than blocking on now.

Experiment description:
Placement: New intermediary entry page inserted before the "All Products" PLP. Shoppers land here first instead of going straight into the full product grid.

Hypothesis:
IF we insert a "What brings you here?" entry page with a Category/Situation toggle before the full PLP, letting shoppers self-select a category or situational need before seeing any products,
THEN we will see an increase in Purchase conversion rate (H1) and add to cart rate (H2), particularly among situational, low-intent browsers,
BECAUSE pre-filtering by need reduces choice overload (Hick's Law) for the ~80% of traffic that arrives without a clear product in mind. Matching entry to why someone is shopping (rather than what they already know they want) gives shoppers who don't yet know what they want a relevant, low-effort starting point instead of an undifferentiated grid of 8+ product categories.

Test Name: ID966 | EU | PLP | Flagship - "I'm Shopping For [Category]" Dropdown on PLP
Experiment description:
What the change will be: 
Control: current live PLP header — no persistent category/context selector at the top, standard filter icon and product count only. 

Variant: add a prominent "I'm shopping for [category]" dropdown at the top of the PLP, above the filter/product-count row, defaulting to "All." Selecting a different value from the dropdown re-filters the grid to that category, functioning as a persistent, always-visible alternative (or companion) to the existing filter mechanism. No other PLP elements change.
Hypothesis:
IF we add a persistent "I'm shopping for [category]" dropdown at the top of the PLP,

THEN we will see an increase in PLP → PDP click-through rate and increase in purchase conversion,

BECAUSE framing the selector as a first-person statement of intent ("I'm shopping for...") rather than a generic filter label lowers the cognitive threshold to narrow down 60 undifferentiated products, and keeping it persistently visible at the top (rather than buried in a filter drawer) surfaces the option to self-segment before shoppers have to manually scroll and evaluate a large, unfiltered grid — directly addressing choice overload for browsers without a specific product in mind.

Note the 3 different states: default dropdown, opened dropdown and sticky dropdown when you scroll past it.

Test Name: ID969 | EU | PDP | Remove Bundle & Save block
Experiment description:
The current PDP template includes a "Bundle & save" carousel surfacing curated bundles (Good Night, Daily Calm, Deluxe, Full Coverage) with anchored discount pricing directly on the single-product page. This block is not individually tracked, so its contribution to AOV and sales is inferred rather than measured. As a proxy, we measured how many PDP visitors navigate onward to a specific bundle PDP:

- Dream: 9.2% PDP visitors visit a bundle PDP
- Switch: 10,6
- Experience: 10.7
- Quiet: 10,8
- Engage: 13,5
- All average: 10.6
(see attachment image)

On average 10.6% of PDP visitors move onward to a bundle PDP, with earplug-bundle the dominant destination (54% of all click-throughs, 5.7% of all PDP traffic). This click-through path is not the block's total value — it excludes bundles bought without a bundle-PDP visit and includes visitors who would have found bundles anyway — but it establishes the block sits on a non-trivial share of the journey. The flagship PDP redesign removes this block for a cleaner, more premium layout. Since it is a live cross-sell and value-framing mechanism, removing it blind risks suppressing bundle attach rate and AOV. This test isolates the removal on the current PDP — ahead of the full flagship migration — so its impact on AOV and sales reads cleanly, separate from every other flagship change. Bundle-PDP entries dropping is expected and is not itself the finding; the question is what happens to revenue per visitor.
Hypothesis: If we remove the Bundle & save block from the PDP, then AOV (h2) and will drop while single-product CVR (h1) holds steady, because the block is currently the main way shoppers discover bundles and see their discounted value at the moment they're ready to buy.

Test Name: ID975 | EU | Cart | Empty Cart State — "Empty, For Now" + Recently Viewed Recovery
Experiment description:

THEN Purchase conversion rate will increase (H1) and Add to cart will hold steady (H2), even though the variant has no direct add option on this screen,
BECAUSE most empty cart visits are interrupted shopping trips, not dead ends. One clear route back to the product they were already looking at takes less effort than the quiz or a carousel of products they haven't chosen.

Test Name: ID981 | EU | Quiz | Multi-Select Use Case Question on Quiz Q1
Experiment description:
Control: current live quiz Q1 allows selecting only one use case tile (Noise sensitivity, Music & events, Better sleep, Conversations & social gatherings, Focus & travel, All day noise control, Parenting, Other) before advancing. 

Variant: same question and same tiles, but shoppers can select multiple use cases before proceeding — e.g. someone can pick both "Better sleep" and "Parenting" if both apply. No changes to tile content, imagery, or order; only the selection behavior (single vs. multi) and the underlying recommendation logic needed to weight multiple inputs.
Hypothesis:
IF we allow shoppers to select multiple use cases on Quiz Q1 instead of forcing a single choice,

THEN we will see an increase in quiz completion rate and Results page → Purchase conversion rate,

BECAUSE most real buying situations aren't single-purpose (someone buying for both sleep and parenting, or noise sensitivity and travel, is common) and forcing a single pick creates artificial friction — either shoppers hesitate/abandon because no single tile feels fully accurate (choice-fit anxiety), or they pick one arbitrarily, which degrades match quality and lowers confidence in the final recommendation. Letting them select everything that's true removes that forced trade-off and should produce a more personally relevant — and more trusted — result.

Test Name: ID984 | EU | Sitewide | Mobile nav: Help me choose relocated to level 2 (contextual placement)
Experiment description:
Move the "Help me choose" entry point out of the top-level mobile nav and place it contextually at level 2 inside both Shop by product and Shop by need, providing access to the quiz, compare and read-more routes. 

Do-no-harm: primary KPI is CvR staying flat, freeing level 1 for the new flagship IA.

Changes
- Move "Help me choose" from level 1 of the mobile nav into two level 2 panels; 
    - Add the  "Help me choose" at the foot of both Shop by product and Shop by need panels
        - The link opens the same panel as in control — no change to its contents
            - Panel gives access to the Quiz, the Compare page, and to read and learn more by need

Supporting evidence
- Baymard — mobile nav guidance favours a short, scannable top level with clear category scent; secondary/utility items competing at level 1 dilute the primary paths and increase mis-taps.
- Hick's law / choice overload — fewer top-level options reduces decision time on the most-used routes; the removed item is low-traffic relative to Shop by product/need.
- Progressive disclosure — help is surfaced at the moment of need rather than pre-emptively; contextual placement raises perceived relevance of the same CTA.
- Flagship kickoff Q1/Q4 — directly serves "help visitors find their Loop" and "decisive vs curious without friction": decisive users get an unobstructed product list, curious users get help one tap deeper.
Hypothesis:
IF we relocate the "Help me choose" entry point from level 1 to the foot of both level 2 panels, 
THEN conversion rate (h1) will remain flat while level 1 becomes simpler and guided-selling usage holds, 
BECAUSE users don't recognise a need for help before they've encountered the choice set — the same panel is more relevant one tap deeper, and a shorter level 1 lowers scan cost on the primary shopping paths.

Learnings & recommendations:
Recommendation: Implement Variation 1 (full flagship Dream PDP) in EU and USA. Launch in AUS as well. Fix the cross-sell modules alongside the rollout.
We rebuilt the entire Dream PDP into the flagship direction. The bar was do-no-harm: look premium, don't lose sales. The page cleared that bar comfortably. EU converts 5.3% better, USA 8.9% better, both at 99% chance. Together that is +6.3% at over 99.9% chance. The premium direction is not something we pay for in conversion. It pays us.
The reason is the same in every market: this page is much better at helping people make up their minds. Add to Cart rises everywhere without exception. Compare gets used up to twelve times more. Virtual Try-On clicks are up in all three regions. The elements we used to hide are finally doing work, because people who are still choosing now have something to choose with.
That one idea also explains AUS, where nothing moved. AUS shoppers arrive already decided. Dream is 64% of their basket against 52% in USA, and their control page already converts at 10.6%, nearly double EU. A page built to help people decide has almost nobody left to help. So AUS came out flat: not damaged, just unmoved, and with half the conversions we need for a reliable read there is no signal of harm in either direction.
But the product data tells us something we did not expect, and it is the most useful thing we learned. The page is better at selling Dream and worse at selling anything else. In EU, Dream units rose 11% while every other product together fell 8%. Some of that is fine — people switching from Eclipse or Quiet to Dream keeps the value, and Dream costs more. Two parts are not fine. Loop Link attachments dropped 27%, and Link is a €19 add-on that only ever rides along with another product, so fewer attachments means genuinely smaller baskets. And the whole long tail of products — bundles, multipacks, collabs — lost €1.17 per order, which accounts for the entire EU AOV decline on its own. The best-sellers held their value per order exactly. The loss is all in the tail.
So the honest summary is this: we built a page that converts better and cross-sells worse. The best-sellers held their value per order exactly. The loss is all in the tail.
So the honest summary is this: we built a page that converts better and cross-sells worse. The first effect is much bigger than the second — EU revenue per user is still up 3.3% and revenue up €6,383 in 16 days — so we go ahead. But the second effect is a design problem with a design fix, and we should not launch and forget it.
Management summary: The flagship Dream PDP wins because it helps undecided shoppers decide — +6.3% conversion across EU and USA — and it left Australia flat only because those shoppers already arrive with their minds made up.

Test Name: ID1002 | EU | Sitewide | Flagship Mobile Nav 2026
Experiment description:
Replace the entire mobile navigation with the 2026 flagship design: dark-themed, tabbed, with two parallel level-1 shopping routes (product-type and situation), a five-situation taxonomy, visual product cards, a sub-panel for products with a Plus version, and per-situation editorial guides.

Do-no-harm: primary KPI is CvR staying flat.

The real deliverable is an elevated nav with a full picture of nav usage in both control and v1 - every link (to a page) is ideally tracked with a query code - so the flagship IA can be validated before it becomes the redesign baseline.

Changes from Control
1. Level 1 restructured from a shop and help (guided selling) mix into two routes plus utility: Shop by product, Shop by situation, Accessories, Bundles (Save up to 20%), Shop all, and Returns & cancellations below a divider.
2. Shop by product opens an intermediate "By products" panel — Earplugs, Sleep masks, Baby earmuffs, each with thumbnail — plus Compare, Shop all and Help me choose.
    a. This is a risk, as user-journey lengthens vs Control - BUT it is important as it supports brand product category growth
    b. Sleep masks links to: /products/eclipse
    c. Baby earmuffs links to: /products/cocoon
        i. No sold out tag at this spot, it would look too prominent here - and it is handled at PDP via a notify me feature, so no dead end. 
3. Plus becomes a variant panel, not a separate SKU row. Loop Engage and Loop Experience open their own panel with the base product and the Plus version, labelled "Includes Loop Mute", plus Shop all and Help me choose. Dream, Switch, Quiet and Engage Kids link straight to their product page.
4. Tabs added at the top of the drawer: Shop / What's new / About us (control has no tab layer). What's new carries three editorial cards — Paris Hilton x Loop Engage, Loop Eclipse, Amnesia Ibiza x Loop — ordered to match the homepage hero carousel, plus Collaborations, Limited editions, Shop all and a Partnerships section.
5. Dark theme replaces white.
6. "Shop by need" → "Shop by situation"  and the taxonomy collapses from nine to five: Sleep, Focus, Noise sensitivity, Events & music, Kids.
7. Situation panels become visual: product cards with imagery and one-line descriptors, plus Compare and Shop all. Situation panels link to base products only — no variant drill-down.
8. Editorial guides added at the foot of situation panels: Sleep guide + White noise generator (Sleep), Work & study guide (Focus), Parenting guide + Noise sensitivity guide (Noise sensitivity), Concert guide + Festival guide (Events & music), Kids' hearing guide (Kids). No read-time labels.     
9. "Help me choose" is a persistent CTA button at the fo        ot of the By products, Earplugs, Loop Engage, Loop Experience and By situation panels — five placements. Not on level-3 situation panels.
10. Products labelled by benefit in the Earplugs panel: Dream–Restful sleep, Engage–Easier conversations, Experience–Clearer live music, Switch–Adjustable control, Quiet–Deep noise reduction, Engage Kids–Ages 6–12.
11. Product naming: 
    a. full "Loop [Name]™" format,
    b. The "2" number in the names are dropped - we no longer need the generation suffixes 
12. Bundles opens a panel with two NON visual items - using the same copy as Control:
    a. Build your own bundle
        i. Mix and match to save
        ii. Points to /products/build-your-bundle
    b. All Bundles
        i. Our most-loved bundles
        ii. Points to /collections/bundles
13. Footer utility on all three tabs: 
    a. Stores, 
    b. locale switcher, currency switcher
        i. clicking any of the 3 local items will open the same modal that opens from the header Flag on control

⚠️if possible - Full link-level instrumentation in both arms so click distribution is directly comparable - se Dev details field:

Data - Supporting evidence
- Recognition over recall — product imagery in nav panels lets shoppers identify by appearance rather than decoding names; strongest where SKU names are non-descriptive (Quiet, Switch, Engage all read as abstract).
- Hick's law / category-logic consistency (Baymard) — nine mixed entries (need + context + attribute) → six single-logic entries reduces scan and disambiguation cost.
- Dual-path IA (Flagship kickoff Q4, decisive vs. curious) — product-type at level 1 serves the decisive shopper; Shop by situation and the Help me choose CTA serve the curious without diverting the primary path.
- Scalable architecture (Q6) — Earplugs / Sleep masks / Baby earmuffs as top-level categories is the structure that absorbs new lines without another IA rebuild. Eclipse and Halo currently sit awkwardly inside an earplug-shaped nav.
- Editorial in nav is a known risk — content links inside a shopping drawer are a documented diversion vector. These need their own guardrail, not just a CvR floor.
Hypothesis:
IF we replace the current mobile nav with the flagship 2026 design, 

THEN conversion rate will remain flat - validating the new Flagship nav design

BECAUSE the IA gives decisive shoppers a product route and undecided shoppers a situation route and Help me choose at relevant placements, instead of one mixed list; visual cards let people recognise products rather than decode names; nesting Plus under its parent frames it as an upgrade, and five situations built on real intended use cases cut the work of choosing.

Watch: products now sit a level down, Engage and Experience two. Added depth could suppress product-panel entry and PDP visits even if CvR holds.

- Scalable architecture (Q6) — Earplugs / Sleep masks / Baby earmuffs as top-level categories is the structure that absorbs new lines without another IA rebuild. Eclipse and Halo currently sit awkwardly inside an earplug-shaped nav.
- Editorial in nav is a known risk — content links inside a shopping drawer are a documented diversion vector. These need their own guardrail, not just a CvR floor.

IF we replace the current mobile nav with the flagship 2026 design, 

THEN conversion rate will remain flat - validating the new Flagship nav design

BECAUSE the IA gives decisive shoppers a product route and undecided shoppers a situation route and Help me choose at relevant placements, instead of one mixed list; visual cards let people recognise products rather than decode names; nesting Plus under its parent frames it as an upgrade, and five situations built on real intended use cases cut the work of choosing.

Test Name: ID1008 | EU | BYOB | BYOB 2.0: goal-based sticky footer
Experiment description:
Remove the four-node discount ladder from the top of Build Your Own Bundle and move progress into the sticky footer as a single next-goal message, with the max saving carried by a new hero sub-headline. 
List rows unchanged. 

Do-no-harm: primary KPI is CvR staying flat on BYOB-entered sessions, with bundle size and AOV as a signal.

Changes
- Hero - new background image and gains sub-headline "Save up to 20%" — carries the ceiling the ladder used to communicate
- Four-node stepper removed, along with the sticky top band and the redundant 'Buld your Bundle' copy; product list now starts directly under the hero
    - Sticky footer rebuilt, showing one goal state at a time as a pill with sparkle icon: "Add 2 items to start saving" (when user has 0–1 items)
    - "10% off unlocked · Spend £X more for 15%"
    - "15% off unlocked · Spend £X more for 20%"
    - "20% off unlocked!"
- Footer adds a "You'll save £X" line in red above the subtotal
- Subtotal gains a superscript item count
- Expand chevron retained on the bundle summary, but 'Expand' copy removed
- Row UI, swatches, Add pill and See details all unchanged from control

Supporting evidence
- Goal-gradient effect (Kivetz, Urminsky & Zheng, 2006) — the core mechanism. Effort accelerates as a goal nears; a single reachable target should raise the rate at which shoppers cross the next threshold.
- Anchoring (BOOM day 5) — the ladder puts €99 in view immediately. For someone holding one €54.95 item that reads as far off, and risks reframing the exercise as expensive rather than rewarding.
- Loss framing — "You'll save £5.99" makes the discount a concrete quantity in hand rather than a percentage in the abstract; "10% unlocked" creates something to protect.
- Proximity / co-location — decision-relevant information beside the decision. The control's progress cue sits at the top of a long scroll, far from the point of commitment.
- Cognitive load — four simultaneous thresholds, two mechanisms and a price ladder is a lot to parse above the fold on mobile.
- Above-fold recovery — removing the sticky top surfaces roughly one extra product on first view, which supports the range exposure that drives bundle size.

Risk - we no logner communicate free shipping
Hypothesis:
IF we replace the four-node ladder with a single next-goal message placed in the sticky footer, 

THEN conversion rate will remain flat while bundle size, threshold-crossing rate and AOV hold or improve,

BECAUSE showing all four thresholds at once anchors on the largest unreached target and makes saving feel distant to a shopper holding one item; a single proximate goal exploits the goal-gradient effect, where effort rises as perceived distance to reward shrinks. Moving the message into the footer also co-locates it with the subtotal and the CTA, so the "is one more item worth it" calculation happens where the shopper is already looking rather than requiring a scroll back to the top.
