Test Name: ID1012 | EU | Cart | Cart New Design Cross-Sell Block
Experiment description:
Control: Small square product thumbnail on the left, with name, colour label and colour swatch stacked to its right. Price shown as an increment ("+ €34.95") and the Add button share a row at the bottom. The thumbnail is about the same size as the product already in the cart. One card fits the width, with about a fifth of the next one showing.

Variant: A single large product card. The image is centred at the top and much bigger, sitting directly on the white card with no grey container behind it. Name, colour label and swatch move below the image, full width, with a smaller swatch. Price is shown on its own ("€34.95") rather than as an increment. The Add button is unchanged. The card is wider and taller, so barely any of the next card shows and the block reads as one product at a time. It also sits higher in the cart and takes up about a quarter more space.

Isolation note: Per your scope, the block title/headline is unchanged and the underlying recommendation logic (which products are shown) is unchanged. The only variable is the visual design of the card itself — image size/prominence, layout hierarchy, and browsing mechanic (arrows + horizontal list vs. swipe + dot pagination). Any other differences visible across the two screenshots (progress bar, USP row, Apple Pay button, "Your cart" vs "Your bag" label) are outside this test.
Hypothesis:
IF we redesign the cross-sell block from a small thumbnail with dense text into a large single product card (full changes in the description above),

THEN more shoppers will add a recommended product, lifting cart AOV (H2), while purchase conversion rate holds steady (H1). Overall add-to-cart rate as guardrail.

BECAUSE the control undersells the product at the moment someone is deciding on an impulse add. A small thumbnail with several bits of information crammed into one row makes the shopper work to take it in, and the product itself barely registers. A big image does the selling for you. That matters more here than on a product page, where people already intend to buy. Showing one product at a time may also hold attention better than a row of small cards that invites scrolling straight past.

KPI note: cross-sell add-to-cart rate was the original H1, but the sample size is too small to decide on. Only ~685 cross-sell adds per arm (out of 197k users), so the metric could only have detected a change of roughly 15% or more. The observed change was -2.9%. Reassigned to a learning metric before read-out; purchase CR takes over as H1.

Visitor archetypes most affected: Satisficers moving quickly through the cart, who are more likely to be swayed by one strong product image than by scanning a row of small ones. Likely limited effect on Rejectors who don't engage with cross-sell at all.

- Metric on add to cart of the xsell items (control & variant)

Learnings & recommendations:
Recommendations:
- Keep control in all regions — the country flag stays in the mobile header. No implementation.

Next:
1. After Flagship project - Test fixing entry UX: make the "Are you in the right place?" pop-up more clear - so EU users start in the correct store. 
    a. See M&S UK Copy for inspiration.  
    b. Test as do-no-harm with bounce and CR as guardrail.
2. if (1) works: re-test moving the flag. If it's still a loss then, the flag is about reassurance, not switching — and it stays for good.
3. Extra high-impact optimization idea - for users in the incorrect country - show a top Header Bar to more clearly help them move to the correct country (like the M&S UK solution).

Learnings:
- The header flag does two jobs; nav and footer only do one. It shows which store you're in and lets you change it. Nav and footer only offer the change — and only to users who already know they're in the wrong place and go looking.
- Moving closer helped, but not enough. EU switcher opens: header 2.58% → footer only 0.25% (ID943) → footer + nav 0.80% (ID1016). Still under a third of the header level.
- The loss lands at the last step. ATC, PDP views and checkout entry flat in both tests; the drop only shows at purchase. A mismatched user can still buy — country is changeable at checkout — so this isn't a wall. It's friction (wrong country, shipping and payment options pre-filled) plus lost reassurance: the flag matching your country tells you the store is for you. We can't yet say which weighs more.
- The switcher matters in proportion to how many users start in the wrong store. Modal completion in control: EU 12.68% · AU 2.76% · US 0.43%. Effect of moving the flag: EU loses · AU flat · US flat. Same order. The EU has no auto-redirect and a pop-up that competes with the cookie banner; the US redirects; AU is single-country.
- The ID943 US "win" was noise. +3.3% at 94% CtW became flat (+0.2%, 57%) with 1.7× the users. Read across both tests, the US answer is no harm, not a lift.

Baymard found country overlays are often mistaken for ads and closed unread, and points to geotargeting plus a persistent header flag as the pattern that works. That's our control.

Management summary: Moving the country switcher out of the header made no difference in the USA or Australia — because hardly anyone there needs it. The EU drop decides the design: the flag stays in the header, everywhere - for now.

Test Name: ID1018 | EU | Bundle PDP | Flagship - Earplug Bundle PDP redesign
Experiment description:
Control: Current Earplug bundle PDP on the legacy template — not aligned with the flagship design system

Variant: Earplug bundle PDP rebuilt on the flagship design system — the same components, hierarchy, and visual language being rolled out consistently across all flagship pages — with bundle-specific adaptations layered on top to handle multi-product presentation:
- Flagship-standard layout components (image treatment, typography, CTA style, trust signals, proof placement) — consistent with every other page in the redesign, not bespoke to this page
- Bundle-specific additions the flagship base template doesn't need to handle: per-product breakdown rows (image, name, variant/color selection per item), bundle savings framing, and a single unified add-to-bag action across multiple SKUs
Hypothesis:
IF we rebuild the Earplug bundle PDP on the flagship design system — consistent layout, hierarchy and proof placement with the rest of the site — and add the bundle-specific structure needed to present multiple products clearly (per-item breakdown, savings framing, unified CTA),
 THEN we will see an increase in Purchase CR and bundle ATC, with AOV holding or improving,
 BECAUSE two mechanisms stack here. First, consistency reduces cognitive load (BOOM Day 1, Ability) — a shopper who's already built a mental model of "how Loop PDPs work" elsewhere on the flagship site doesn't have to re-learn a different pattern on the legacy bundle template; less re-orientation effort means less drop-off before they even get to evaluating the bundle. Second, the bundle-specific structure adds Certainty (BOOM Day 4) at the exact point of hesitation unique to multi-product pages — the implicit "what exactly am I getting, and is it worth it vs. buying separately" calculation that a single-SKU-shaped page can't answer.

Archetype framing:
- Decisive buyers benefit most from the consistency piece — no friction from an unfamiliar layout breaking flow between browsing and this page.
- Maximizers benefit most from the bundle-specific piece — the per-item value breakdown gives them the buy-together-vs-separately comparison they're already trying to run mentally, so they resolve it instead of tabbing away.
- Curious shoppers benefit from both — a familiar page structure lowers the barrier to comparing this bundle against other products they've already seen on-site.

Test Name: ID1035 | EU | PDP | Flagship Yotpo follow-up
Experiment description:
Control vs V1 — what changed
Three things added at the top
- AI "Customers say" summary paragraph
- "Read summary by topics" button
- "Reviews with media" photo carousel (2 photos, swipe)
Five things moved to the bottom — from above the reviews to below the reviews and below pagination
- Search reviews box
- Rating dropdown
- With media toggle
- Popular topics pills
- Sort by
Star bars moved down
- Now sit directly above the review list — the intended fix
- Tapping a row re-renders the list right underneath it
- But the proof it worked (active filter state, "We found X matching reviews / Clear filters") now renders at the bottom, out of sight
Background: why a follow-up
ID922 / ID923 / ID924 tested a compressed Yotpo review module on mobile PDPs — padding trimmed, first-page reviews cut from 5 to 3, AI "Customers say" summary added, media gallery enabled, ear-tip-size filter added — and lost in all three markets (purchase CR −2.1% EU, −1.3% USA, −6.5% AUS). The single most consistent finding was that review-filter engagement fell 26.9% in EU, 26.5% in USA and 31.4% in AUS: same direction, same magnitude, three independent samples.

Post-test inspection of the module points at a specific cause. The star-rating distribution is itself a filter — tapping the "3 star" row filters the review list — but in that variant it sat above the AI summary and the media gallery, roughly a full mobile screen away from the reviews it controls. A shopper tapping a star row saw nothing change, because everything that changed was off-screen. An action whose consequence is invisible reads as a broken control: people try it once, conclude it does not work, and stop. That removes the self-service route to the specific reviews that resolve a specific objection — fit being the most-discussed topic in Loop reviews at 11% of all reviews, and explicitly flagged as mixed by Yotpo's own summary.

This test holds the content of the module constant and changes only the sequence: AI summary, then media gallery, then the rating distribution, then the review list. Tapping a star row now visibly re-renders the reviews directly beneath it, within the same viewport. If the hypothesis is accurate, filter interaction should recover toward or above the original module's level, and the conversion and add-to-cart losses from ID922–924 should close.

Two things to keep in mind when reading the result. Control is the original module, not the ID922 variant — so V1 differs from control on content and order. The order-only comparison is this test against ID922 / ID923. And alongside the reorder, the review search box, the filter controls and the keyword topic pills no longer sit above the review list; the AI summary and media gallery take that space instead. So the test also swaps a self-service layer for an AI-served one, and that may act on the same behaviour described above — from a different direction.
Hypothesis:
IF: we move the star-rating distribution directly above the review list on mobile PDPs, so the AI summary and media gallery sit above it rather than between it and the reviews,
THEN: rating-filter interaction will recover, and add-to-cart rate (h2) and purchase conversion rate (h1) will hold or improve,
BECAUSE: the distribution bars are filter controls, and a control whose effect renders off-screen gives no feedback that it worked — shoppers read it as broken and abandon it. Placing the result in the same viewport as the control closes the action–feedback loop, restoring the fastest route to the reviews that answer a shopper's specific doubt.

A shopper tapping a star row saw nothing change, because everything that changed was off-screen. An action whose consequence is invisible reads as a broken control: people try it once, conclude it does not work, and stop. That removes the self-service route to the specific reviews that resolve a specific objection — fit being the most-discussed topic in Loop reviews at 11% of all reviews, and explicitly flagged as mixed by Yotpo's own summary.

This test holds the content of the module constant and changes only the sequence: AI summary, then media gallery, then the rating distribution, then the review list. Tapping a star row now visibly re-renders the reviews directly beneath it, within the same viewport. If the hypothesis is accurate, filter interaction should recover toward or above the original module's level, and the conversion and add-to-cart losses from ID922–924 should close.

Two things to keep in mind when reading the result. Control is the original module, not the ID922 variant — so V1 differs from control on content and order. The order-only comparison is this test against ID922 / ID923. And alongside the reorder, the review search box, the filter controls and the keyword topic pills no longer sit above the review list; the AI summary and media gallery take that space instead. So the test also swaps a self-service layer for an AI-served one, and that may act on the same behaviour described above — from a different direction.
Hypothesis:
IF: we move the star-rating distribution directly above the review list on mobile PDPs, so the AI summary and media gallery sit above it rather than between it and the reviews,
THEN: rating-filter interaction will recover, and add-to-cart rate (h2) and purchase conversion rate (h1) will hold or improve,
BECAUSE: the distribution bars are filter controls, and a control whose effect renders off-screen gives no feedback that it worked — shoppers read it as broken and abandon it. Placing the result in the same viewport as the control closes the action–feedback loop, restoring the fastest route to the reviews that answer a shopper's specific doubt.

Test Name: ID1044 | EU | Homepage | Hero stacked follow-up
Experiment description:
Previous test: ID955 — Homepage Hero Format: Carousel vs Stacked vs Hybrid, mobile, run in EU, USA and AUS [add EU/AUS IDs]. Neither variant was good enough to roll out, least of all in EU, our largest market: stacked came in at −5.9% purchase CR there and hybrid at −3.1%. Pooled across all three markets stacked was −3.8% (~93% likely worse) and hybrid −1.1% (flat). So we iterate rather than roll out.

What we learned
Slide CTR moved a lot and revenue did not. Making slides more visible lifted CTR 2–8x with 100% certainty on nearly every slide, while purchase rate stayed flat or fell. PDP entrance rate did not move either (pooled −0.7%, inconclusive). PLP entrance looked like it rose, but that is the Archive Sale page sitting on a PLP URL path — the extra clicks on the Archive slide alone account for the entire gain, so no real change there.
The read: attention inside the hero is easy to move, and it does not by itself become a product visit or a purchase. The next step has to be about converting hero attention into product entries, not about generating more hero clicks.

Two variations
Both are auto-timed with the pause control available, and both move the evergreen slide from position 5 to position 3 — in the previous test it out-clicked the campaign slide at position 3 in all three markets from a worse position, so its demand is suppressed by placement.
- V1 (design) — visual cleanup, stronger focus on the imagery. Hero height unchanged.
- V2 — same as V1, plus shorter cards so the bestseller product entrance sits higher in the page, and a clear product-linked CTA on each card. Built as a fork of V1, so V1 → V2 isolates card height + CTA.

What we'll learn
- Whether promoting the evergreen slide finally turns its demand into product visits (Control → V1), and on top of that whether a shorter hero with product-linked CTAs converts hero attention into PDP entrances and purchases (V1 → V2). If slide CTR rises again without purchase CR following, that settles it: hero layout is not a revenue lever and we take it off the roadmap.
Hypothesis: If we make the hero visually cleaner and more focused (V1), and shorten the cards while giving each one a clear product-linked CTA (V2), we expect purchase conversion rate (H1) and slider CTR (H2) to increase, because ID955 showed that hero clicks rose sharply while purchase rate, PDP and PLP entrance all stayed flat — the hero produced attention but not qualified product traffic, and it pushed the bestseller product entrance too far down the page.
Dev briefing:
'- Only change the hero format (so no usecase entrys etc, just the top part)
- Same CTR measurement of all slides like in previous test
Analysis results overview:
Purchase CR (H1): both variants slightly lower, not significant.
- Control: 10.56%
- V1: 10.42% (−1.3%, 29% chance to win)
- V2: 10.42% (−1.3%, 29% chance to win)

Hero CTR (H2), all slides combined: big lift, strongest in V2.
- Control: 2.84%
- V1: 4.54% (+60%)
- V2: 6.00% (+111%)
- Per slide: V2 is up on slides 1, 2, 3 and 5 (94–100% chance). V1 is up on slides 1 and 2 but down on slides 3 and 4 (5% and 3% chance to win).

PDP visit rate: no change. More hero clicks did not bring more people to product pages.
- Control: 46.36%
- V1: 45.95% (−0.9%, 16%)
- V2: 46.10% (−0.6%, 26%)

PLP visit rate: V2 is lower.
- Control: 26.55%
- V1: 26.58% (+0.1%, 53%)
- V2: 25.95% (−2.3%, 5%), so 95% likely worse

Add to cart rate: flat to slightly up, not significant.
- Control: 14.40%
- V1: 14.59% (+1.3%, 76%)
- V2: 14.49% (+0.6%, 63%)

AOV: V1 is lower, V2 is flat.
- Control: €55.73
- V1: €54.91 (−1.5%, 6%), so 94% likely lower
- V2: €55.88 (+0.3%, 50%)

RPU: both lower, not significant.
- Control: €5.89
- V1: €5.72 (−2.9%, 12%)
- V2: €5.82 (−1.1%, 31%)

Checkout rate: flat (V1 61%, V2 41% chance to win).
Learnings & recommendations:
What happened:
- The Loop Archive sale changed normal behaviour. A discount gives people a strong reason to tap. The Archive slide was the most-tapped slide in the carousel, and it sent people straight to the sale page. That hides the effect of the design itself, because the deal does the selling, not the hero.
- After the Archive sale ended, the slide order in V1 and V2 changed by mistake. Evergreen should have moved up to 2nd place, but it ended up last. That made the results even harder to read.


So I split the test into period A (24–29 Sep, with the Archive, planned design) and period B (1–5 Oct, no Archive, wrong slide order). All numbers below are all markets combined.
- Hero CTR was up in both variants, in both periods. In period A: V1 +58%, V2 +103%. In period B the lift was smaller: V1 +21%, V2 +54%. Without the sale slide there is simply less to tap.
- Purchases were flat with the sale, and V1 dropped without it. In period A: V1 +1.1%, V2 0.0% (no difference). In period B: V1 −6.8% (clearly worse), V2 −1.0% (still close to control).
- ATC rose a little with the sale and fell without it. In period A: V1 +3.2%, V2 +0.8%. In period B: V1 −4.6%, V2 −3.6%, both worse.
- Slider CTAs: a clear button beats a good position.
    - Evergreen with the quiz CTA (V2) got about 4× more taps than without a CTA (V1), even when it sat in last place.
    - The Archive with "Enter the archive" got the most taps of all.
    - The cleaner top slide (Paris) got about 2.5× more taps in both variants.
    - None of these extra taps led to more purchases.


Why we go with V2 for the big homepage test 
 Think of it like this: both designs look fine when the sale does the work. The real question is what happens when the sale is gone, which is most of the year. V1 then loses purchases. V2 stays close to control and sells about 6% more than V1 under the same conditions. Neither one is a winner, but V2 is the safer bet. Waiting for Heatmap data to confirm.

Advice:
  Use V2 (shorter cards + a CTA on each card) in the full Flagship homepage test, with Evergreen always in 2nd place as designed.
  The hero doesn't drive sales, so fine to go ahead with a branded first slide. Cleaner Paris wins in both in CTR.
Management summary: The new hero designs doubled taps but not sales. During the Archive sale both variants matched control. Once the sale ended, V1 lost purchases (−7%) while V2 stayed level. V2 goes into the full homepage test as the safer option, not as a winner.
